entities.summary:
Matthäus Lang von Wellenburg (died 1540), a preeminent statesman of the Holy Roman Empire and a Cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church, served as Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg from 1519 until his death. His career unfolded during the tumultuous dawn of the Reformation, placing him at the nexus of imperial politics, ecclesiastical authority, and nascent religious dissent. A shrewd diplomat and administrator, Lang was instrumental in solidifying the temporal power of the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg, asserting its territorial integrity and political influence within the fragmented imperial landscape, often aligning its interests with the burgeoning might of the Habsburg dynasty under Emperors Maximilian I and Charles V.

Elevated to Cardinal by Pope Julius II in 1511 and subsequently Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg, Lang navigated the complex currents of early 16th-century European politics. He played a crucial role in the imperial diets, notably at Augsburg and Worms, where he advocated for Catholic orthodoxy and sought to mitigate the spread of Lutheranism. His administrative reforms in Salzburg aimed at strengthening both the spiritual and secular governance of his see, including efforts to modernize its legal and economic structures. Lang's political acumen was particularly evident in his involvement in the election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519, where he leveraged his influence to secure Habsburg succession and further embed Salzburg within the imperial framework.

entities.summary:
Matthäus Lang von Wellenburg (1468, Augsburg – April 9, 1540) ascended from humble origins to become a preeminent statesman of the Holy Roman Empire, a cardinal, and the Prince-Archbishop of Salzburg from 1519 until his death. His career spanned the crucial transition from the late Medieval period to the early modern era, marked by the rise of the Habsburg dynasty, the burgeoning Renaissance, and the explosive onset of the Protestant Reformation. A trusted advisor to Emperor Maximilian I and later Charles V, Lang leveraged his shrewd diplomatic skills and administrative acumen to consolidate power for the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg and to navigate the complex political and religious currents of his time, making him a central, albeit often controversial, figure in Central European history.

Lang's ecclesiastical and political rise was meteoric; he served as secretary to Emperor Frederick III and later became a key confidant to Maximilian I, who elevated him to bishop of Gurk in 1505 and coadjutor of Salzburg in 1512. His cardinalate, conferred by Pope Leo X in 1518, underscored his diplomatic importance, particularly in brokering the election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor in 1519. As Prince-Archbishop, Lang vigorously pursued the suppression of early Protestant movements within his territories, notably during the Salzburg Peasants' War of 1525-1526, where he was famously besieged in Hohensalzburg Fortress. He also initiated significant architectural projects, expanding the fortress and contributing to Salzburg's urban development, solidifying the temporal and spiritual authority of his see.
